title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) assessing whether inserting an executable emulator validator with a bounded repair policy (guarded) changes the semantic failure rate compared with an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic shared-generation paired design we produced one initial candidate per intent→configuration task with gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions for N=120 paired tasks (40 per topology class). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency n_11 = 120, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We revise the manuscript in response to peer review by (1) providing a compact formal definition of the binary outcome and its decision logic grounded in archived scorer/validator fields; (2) adding a concise nearest-work comparison matrix that explicitly contrasts design choices; (3) tightening the shared-generation design framing and experimental implications; and (4) clarifying operational and validity limitations and reproducibility pointers to archived artifacts.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into concrete device-level commands but may produce sequences that are syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe in closed-loop enactment (for example, violating make-before-break or group-availability constraints). Prior work therefore recommends layering verification, emulation, or veto layers between generation and enactment to detect and prevent such semantic failures. We designed a preregistered paired experiment to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The confirmatory research question is: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: for each task a single generator output was scored both as baseline (LLM-only) and as guarded (validator±repair). This design removes generator-induced variance across paired episodes and therefore measures only the validator/repair subsystem's incremental effect; the trade-off is clear: if the generator produces valid candidates for the selected task bank, repair will be unused and the confirmatory test cannot demonstrate an intervention benefit. We report execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, an explicit formalization of the pass/fail mapping used in analysis, a compact nearest-work comparison, and concrete design recommendations for future follow-ups.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation-grounded benchmarks and NetOps verification tools have emphasized closed-loop failure classes that text-only checks miss (sequencing, dependency, group-availability) and have motivated tool-augmented LLM architectures and guarded pipelines. Representative verified works include recent executable-benchmark efforts that run closed-loop emulation and papers proposing guarded agent designs and generate→validate→repair workflows (see cited record ids below). Prior comparative evaluations often conflate generator variability with verification efficacy (independent per-condition generation) or focus on generator-only metrics; by contrast, our paired shared-generation design isolates validator marginal effects. Table 2 (nearest-work comparison) succinctly contrasts prior experiments with our design along key axes: shared vs independent generation, executable validator presence, repair budget, task provenance, and model diversity. This compact matrix shows that our methodological contribution is primarily experimental design: a preregistered, artifact-rich paired protocol holding generation fixed to measure validator/repair marginal effects under identical generator outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before execution. Key preregistered elements used without post-hoc changes: paired-binary design with N=120 distinct tasks (40 per topology class), primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, exact two-sided McNemar as the prespecified confirmatory test, and a bootstrap-percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified deterministic task generation, validator semantics, repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), contamination rules, deterministic emulator reset, and sensitivity analyses.

Task generation, harness, and staged shared-generation. Tasks were produced deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, and a structured required_sequence that the validator enforces. For each pair we executed a single shared initial generation with declared model gpt-5-mini (execution manifest: model_calls_used = 120; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 120). The harness recorded provider-call audits, deterministic emulator resets (container image checksums and deterministic seeds), and contamination heuristics (duplicate-output checks, cross-condition cache key reuse); none triggered exclusions. Planned_episode_count = 240 (baseline+guarded), completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0.

Validator semantics and scoring rule (formalized). The binary label mapped to the preregistered pass/fail outcome is defined as follows (all fields and identifiers are present in archived scoring artifacts):
- Scorer and rule: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applying scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation".
- Decision logic (binary label S ∈ {0,1}): S = 1 (success/pass) iff scorer.score == 1 AND validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0. S = 0 (failure) iff any of: scorer.score != 1 OR validator_trace.validation_after.valid == false OR validator_trace.violation_count > 0. Repair was triggered when validator_trace.violation_count > 0; preregistered policy allowed at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. This mapping directly corresponds to fields present in archived JSON scoring artifacts (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json contains scorer.score = 1, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, violation_count = 0).

Shared-generation rationale and known risk. Holding the generator fixed isolates validator/repair effects but reduces the probability of encountering generator-induced invalid candidates when the generator+prompt are well-matched to the task bank—a risk explicitly acknowledged in the preregistration.
sections.results:
Primary outcome and contingency. The run completed without technical exclusions (complete_pair_count = 120). Condition-level summaries: baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar test: p = 1.0. Paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces recorded repair_applied = false in all guarded episodes and validator.violation_count = 0 for every pair; consequently no repair-provider traces were produced.

Per-topology counts. The preregistered partition produced 40 pairs per topology class; per-topology results were:
- Edge: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40 (success rate 1.00)
- Core: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40 (success rate 1.00)
- Leaf–spine: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40 (success rate 1.00)
These counts come from the task_manifest entries and archived scoring artifacts (representative artifacts: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and -guarded.json).

Representative pass example (archived). Task pair pair-000001 illustrates a pass: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer; scorer.score = 1; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.violation_count = 0; score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION". This concrete artifact demonstrates the exact field values that produce S = 1 under our decision logic.

Absence of fail artifacts and consequence. No archived scoring artifact records a fail or repair_applied = true in this run. Therefore the confirmatory test is degenerate (zero discordant pairs): the observed ceiling outcome is an empirical fact of this generator+task-bank+prompt configuration and not an artifact of analysis. The preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating technical exclusions as failures) were unnecessary because there were no technical exclusions (analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling result. The paired shared-generation protocol cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects: because the generator outputs for the selected task bank satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in every pair, the guarded subsystem was never exercised and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI reflect this ceiling. This empirical outcome highlights a design lesson: a shared-generation design is appropriate when the objective is to measure only the verifier/repair marginal effect on identical candidates, but it will be statistically uninformative if the generator rarely produces invalid candidates under the frozen prompt.

Design trade-offs and concrete recommendations for follow-ups. Based on archived task difficulty metadata (fields dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the observed absence of repairs, we recommend preregistered adjustments for confirmatory studies that aim to measure repair utility:
1) Independent per-condition generation: permit separate generator draws per condition to expose generator variance and increase discordant-pair incidence; match randomization or blocking to preserve comparability.
2) Targeted task selection: preregister emphasis on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to raise the prior probability that generators produce invalid candidates.
3) Controlled prompt perturbations: prespecify perturbation variants for a subset of tasks to increase generator errors while maintaining a paired structure for complementary blocks.
4) Expanded repair budget in exploratory arms: allow >1 repair iteration to study convergence behavior and cost of repair calls.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (which the archived artifacts demonstrate) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis: the harness recorded provider-call audits, validator traces, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts that enable third-party inspection of decision logic and accounting. However, claims about repair utility must be bounded: if the generator is well-calibrated to the task bank the guard will be idle by design.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; some production-specific behaviors and partial-observability failure classes are not modeled. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single declared model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline failure ≈0.40 and targeted 0.15 reduction) were violated by observed baseline = 0.00; consequently the confirmatory test could not evaluate the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment (N=120) holding the generator fixed to evaluate whether an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline reduces semantic failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow. All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding concordant success for both conditions (n_11 = 120), a paired-difference estimate of 0.00, McNemar p = 1.0, and a degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The primary scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate a preregistered, artifact-rich paired protocol that isolates validator/repair marginal effects and provide concrete, artifact-grounded recommendations for future confirmatory designs that aim to measure repair utility under generator variance. All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts supporting these results are archived and checksummed; researchers can use the task_manifest difficulty fields and archived traces to design follow-up experiments (for example, selecting higher-difficulty tasks or enabling independent per-condition generation).

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
